newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Renault likely to end 96 in the red.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Renault likely to end 96 in the red.

text.p: Renault SA looks headed for a full year loss after reporting poor first-half results and predicting a difficult second half for both its car and truck operations.

Chairman Louis Schweitzer said the company would probably end the year in the red as cost-cutting efforts were unlikely to compensate for persistent weakness in the European car market and a price war that has eroded its profit margins.
Renault shares fell nearly five percent on the Paris bourse as analysts cut their earnings forecasts after the disappointing first-half results and the company's gloomy prognosis.
On Tuesday Renault reported its net attributable profit shrank to 158 million francs ($30.57 million) in the first six months of the year from 1.76 billion a year earlier.

Its car operation, stuck in the red since the second half of 1995, ran up a 911 million franc loss in the first half of 1996. The truck division's income dwindled to 26 million francs from 519 million and was expected to lose money in the second half.

"The truck operations are not improving. The car unit will fare better, but not sufficiently as the two positive factors -- cost reductions and a renewed model range -- will not compensate for the price war," Schweitzer told the newspaper Le Monde.
The price war's savagery was reflected in the fact that the new Renault Clio was priced lower than its predecessor. Renault also foreswore the automatic yearly price hikes on new models.
Its truck operation was hurt by lower sales in the United States, where the industry is coming off the peak of its cycle. A recovery forecast for the European market has not occurred.

Among the analysts trimming their forecasts was Lehman Brothers' Christopher Will, who lowered his earnings per share (EPS) estimate to a loss of one franc for 1996 from a profit of three francs. "The company is more or less saying to people, 'We are going to lose money this year'," Will said.
Schweitzer said the group would cut jobs again next year after eliminating 1,640 posts in 1996 and bring wages closer in line to those of its rival PSA Peugeot Citroen in a bid to reduce costs.

But analysts who met him on Wednesday morning to discuss the first-half results were disappointed that he had not announced more aggressive measures. "He said the same things he said in March, nothing new," one analyst said.
He lowered his EPS estimates for the group to a loss of 1.7 francs for 1996, down from a profit of 1.5 francs previously, and to a profit of 1.2 francs for 1997, down from 4.8 francs.

Analysts said any savings from cost-reductions were likely to go toward further price cuts to allow Renault to regain 10 percent of the European car market. Its market share fell in the first half to 9.7 percent from 10.6 percent.
"The savings will be used to cut prices and regain market share rather than to improving profitability," one analyst said.
Renault's stock was down 4.96 percent in late trading at 114 francs after recovering from a session low of 109.70 -- close to its all-time low of 107 francs.
The shares were first sold to retail investors in 1994 at 165 francs in the first stage of the group's privatisation.
Renault officially entered the private sector in July when the state reduced its stake to below 50 percent by placing six percent with institutional investors at 139 francs per share.

Many investors have been quietly hoping that the management would adopt more brutal tactics now that the company was private to improve returns. A French analyst said that at Wednesday's meeting, "the Anglo-Saxon analysts were very aggressive."
